title: Lactylation in Desmoplastic Tumours: A Metabolic-Epigenetic Axis Linking Stromal Remodelling, Immune Suppression and Therapy Resistance
content: Dense extracellular matrix deposition, stromal activation and impaired perfusion can create tumour niches that favour lactate accumulation. Lysine lactylation (Kla) provides a molecular link between lactate metabolism, gene expression and protein function, with potential implications for tumour progression and treatment response. Here, we review histone and non-histone lactylation in desmoplastic and stroma-rich tumour contexts, encompassing pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma alongside selected settings in gastric, colorectal, triple-negative breast and hepatocellular cancers. This framework recognises that stromal features vary within and between these malignancies. We synthesise evidence linking lactylation to cancer stemness, fibroblast activation, stromal remodelling and immune suppression, and examine how these processes contribute to therapeutic resistance. Recurrent mechanisms include metabolic adaptation, enhanced DNA repair, suppression of cell death and impaired antitumour immunity. However, lactylation effects depend on the modified protein, lysine residue and cellular context, and are not uniformly tumour-promoting. We critically assess limitations in chemical discrimination, antibody specificity and causal inference, particularly the difficulty of distinguishing Kla-dependent mechanisms from other effects of lactate metabolism. We also discuss therapeutic strategies targeting lactate availability, lactylation enzymes and individual substrates. Most evidence remains preclinical, highlighting the need for quantitative, site-specific and spatially resolved analyses, functional validation and prospective clinical studies. Establishing which lactylation events directly influence tumour behaviour and treatment response will be essential for translating these findings into selective therapies and clinically informative biomarkers.
